lessons.title: LINQ in Depth: Projection, Grouping, and Joins
lessons.content:
# LINQ in Depth: Projection, Grouping, and Joins

LINQ is a set of extension methods on `IEnumerable<T>` that turn loops into declarative pipelines. Foundations covered `Where` and `Select`; this is the rest of the toolbox.

## The dataset for this lesson

```csharp
record Order(int Id, string Customer, string Category, decimal Total, DateOnly Placed);

var orders = new List<Order>
{
    new(1, "Ada",   "Books",  349m, new(2026, 1, 12)),
    new(2, "Ada",   "Tools",  1299m, new(2026, 2, 3)),
    new(3, "Linus", "Books",  199m, new(2026, 2, 14)),
    new(4, "Grace", "Tools",  899m, new(2026, 3, 1)),
    new(5, "Linus", "Coffee", 89m,  new(2026, 3, 9)),
};
```

## Grouping and aggregation

```csharp
var byCustomer = orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.Customer)
    .Select(g => new
    {
        Customer = g.Key,
        Orders   = g.Count(),
        Spend    = g.Sum(o => o.Total),
        Largest  = g.Max(o => o.Total),
    })
    .OrderByDescending(x => x.Spend);

foreach (var row in byCustomer)
    Console.WriteLine($"{row.Customer,-6} {row.Orders} orders, {row.Spend:0} kr");
// Ada    2 orders, 1648 kr
// Grace  1 orders, 899 kr
// Linus  2 orders, 288 kr
```

`GroupBy` returns `IGrouping<TKey, TElement>`, which *is* an `IEnumerable<TElement>` with a `Key` bolted on. That is why you can call `Sum`, `Count`, and `Max` directly on `g`.

## Joins and flattening

```csharp
record Customer(string Name, string City);
var customers = new[] { new Customer("Ada", "Stockholm"), new Customer("Linus", "Göteborg") };

var joined = customers.Join(
    orders,
    c => c.Name,            // outer key
    o => o.Customer,        // inner key
    (c, o) => new { c.City, o.Total });

var flattened = orders
    .GroupBy(o => o.Category)
    .SelectMany(g => g.Take(1));      // first order in each category, one flat sequence
```

`SelectMany` is `Select` followed by "unwrap one level of nesting", the way to turn a sequence of sequences into a single flat one.

## The two families of operators

| Deferred (lazy) | Immediate (executes now) |
| --- | --- |
| `Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`, `Take`, `Skip`, `GroupBy`, `Distinct` | `ToList`, `ToArray`, `ToDictionary`, `Count`, `Sum`, `First`, `Any` |

```csharp
var query = orders.Where(o => { Console.WriteLine($"checking {o.Id}"); return o.Total > 200m; });
Console.WriteLine("query built");   // nothing has run yet
var list = query.ToList();          // NOW the predicate runs, once per element
```

Deferred execution means the query is a recipe, not a result. Enumerate the same query twice and the work happens twice.

## Safe terminal operators

```csharp
var first = orders.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Total > 5000m);   // null, no exception
var single = orders.Single(o => o.Id == 3);                // throws if 0 or 2+ matches
var page = orders.OrderBy(o => o.Placed).Skip(2).Take(2);  // paging
```

> [!WARNING]
> `First()` throws `InvalidOperationException` on an empty sequence; `FirstOrDefault()` returns `null` (or `default`). Neither is "safer", they just fail differently. Use `First` when an empty result is a bug and `FirstOrDefault` when it is a valid outcome you handle.

lessons.title: Final Project: A Task API with ASP.NET Core and EF Core
lessons.content:
# Final Project: A Task API with ASP.NET Core and EF Core

Build a working REST API that ties together everything in this course: LINQ, async, DI, configuration, and EF Core.

## Requirements

1. **The project.** `dotnet new web`, targeting the current LTS. Nullable reference types on, warnings treated as errors.
2. **The model and context.** A `TaskItem` entity (`Id`, `Title`, `Done`, `Due` as `DateOnly`, `CreatedUtc`) and an `AppDbContext` on SQLite. Create the schema with `dotnet ef migrations add` plus `dotnet ef database update`, not with `EnsureCreated`.
3. **A store behind an interface.** `ITaskStore` with fully async methods, every one taking a `CancellationToken` and passing it through to EF Core. Register it as scoped and inject it into your endpoints.
4. **CRUD endpoints under a group.** `MapGroup("/tasks")` with `GET /`, `GET /{id:int}`, `POST /`, `PUT /{id:int}`, `DELETE /{id:int}`. Return the correct status codes: 200, 201 with a Location header, 204, 400, and 404.
5. **Query and paging on the list endpoint.** Support `?done=true`, `?search=text`, `?page=2&pageSize=20`, and `?sort=due`. Build it as a single deferred LINQ query so only the final page is fetched from the database.
6. **A summary endpoint.** `GET /tasks/summary` returns counts by state and overdue count using `GroupBy` and `CountAsync`, computed in SQL rather than in memory.
7. **Configuration, not constants.** Read the connection string and a `MaxPageSize` option from configuration, bind the option with `IOptions<T>`, and keep the development connection string in user secrets.
8. **Real error handling.** Validate the incoming DTO and return `Results.ValidationProblem` on bad input. Add an exception-handling middleware that turns unhandled exceptions into a ProblemDetails response, and log every request with its duration.

## Stretch goals

- Add a `GET /tasks/stream` endpoint returning `IAsyncEnumerable<TaskItem>` and confirm the client receives rows before the query has finished.
- Add integration tests with `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` and an in-memory or temporary SQLite database.
- Add a background service (`BackgroundService`) that logs the overdue count every minute, honouring its stopping token.
- Add OpenAPI metadata (`WithName`, `Produces<T>`) and serve a Swagger UI in Development only.

Submit a link to your finished repository below. An instructor will review it before you can mark this lesson complete.
